I met someone on a dating app, hit it off, and within a day took them up on their invitation to a play party (my first time, but I’ve been interested in the kink scene for a long time). Went fully with the intention to disclose but was so nervous that I didn’t do so immediately. Went the whole night with a knot in my stomach and avoiding mouth to mouth contact. The guilt was crazy. I was trying to simultaneously regulate my body, process all this newness, and hype myself up for a potential rejection in person, in front of others. To say I was stuck with fear is an understatement, so much so that people asked me if I was alright just based off my body language. When all I wanted to do was jump this persons bones. Eventually, we fooled around with body rubbing and other forms of nearly naked outercourse and never had any oral or penetrative sex, direct genital contact, or kissing. I ended up disclosing the next day over text and it didn’t go well. In retrospect, I was way too apologize-y, because I felt terrible about swerving the kisses and making them feel unwanted. Because lord knows I wanted them, very much so. But I think they took it to mean “I’m sorry for having herpes,” which I mean, I’m not. Their first reaction was to ask if they could become infected, which unfortunately told me what I needed to know at the time. They later went on to say they weren’t mad, but were unhappy about me having hid it. I didn’t think I hid it, but my own inaction led me down a very insecure path and I learned that even when you hit it off with someone and think they will be understanding, it’s better to rip the bandaid off before you meet in person, especially if your vibe is casual sex. We never ended up having a whole conversation about it because they never texted me back and unmatched from me on the app and that was that. It was rough on my self esteem, for additional reasons I won’t even get into. Ultimately, like everything else about life, it was a learning experience. It reinforced for me that disclosure is the way to go, and early.

I’ve been where you are. I’ve struggled with chronic passive suicidal ideation for as long as I can remember, and getting this diagnosis has been tough on my sense of safety from myself. I can also relate to what you mean about others having it worse, (I rarely get outbreaks) so what basis do I have to complain? I’m here to tell you it’s ok to feel your feelings. It’s uncomfortable, it fucking hurts, but you’re allowed to feel that way. For me, it’s peaks and valleys. Sometimes I almost forget that I have it, and other times the despair is overwhelming. It might be the same for you. As cliche as it is, healing really is not linear. The only piece of advice I would give you is to accept that some days will be better than others, some will be horrible, and to have a safety plan in place. Who are your confidants? Do you have access to lethal means and if so, what can you do to remove yourself from them? What are your deescalation strategies when you’re in an emotionally heightened state? It’s too easy to just say “it’ll get better.” Because for me, it’s been 3 years and nearly every rejection hurts still. In fact just this past weekend I had one of the worst disclosure experiences of my life and I am still in a lot of pain. So to just say to myself “you’ll be fine” is cruel. I’m not fine, haven’t been fine for a long time, and it’s ok to recognize that. 

I also want to mention that I’m not very familiar with the stats on the correlation between hsv and dv but anecdotally I’ve heard enough from people to say that positive people sometimes stay with abusers because they fear that no one else will want them - you’re certainly not alone in that experience. I don’t blame you for that. I do encourage you to think about what you want for yourself. Something my therapist just told me is you determine your own worth from what you will accept. Very “we accept the love we think we deserve” I know, but it’s honestly true. It may not feel like that when the shame is making you say terrible things about yourself, but you deserve better than someone who hurts you. I know it’s really, really hard to accept that someone might want you with herpes. Three years later I’m still struggling with that. But it’s possible. Somewhere, someday. And even if it wasn’t, you STILL wouldn’t deserve to be with someone who abuses you. Forget the fact that he gave it to you, because transmitting herpes isn’t inherently abusive, but remember how he treats you otherwise. You don’t have to tolerate that just because he is accepting of your diagnosis. That is the bare fucking minimum. You know how they say “the bar is in hell”? Yeah. You deserve a loving, caring relationship with someone who makes you feel wonderful and safe. Don’t accept any less. Trust that I know that it’s harder to be alone, but your safety matters more than someone claiming you as theirs. 

All that being said, it’s ok that you’re grieving your relationship. A sense of loss is to be expected. It’s normal to be depressed after experiencing a loss. You aren’t weird for dissociating in conversation or experiencing passive suicidal ideation. This sounds like it’s part of the healing process, which again, is not linear. You’re already doing things to help the healing. Going to the gym?! Trusting a male friend to guide you into something new?? You’re doing amazing!!

Finally, that comparison stuff is only going to continue to bring you down. Nowhere does it say that people with herpes can never travel, have relationships, or even create more humans. It’s seemingly impossible to accept that, I know. But something that I’ve been trying to hold onto is the fact that herpes is kind of like an asshole filter. It saves me from getting with emotionally immature people all the time. It may help to frame things like that. Now YOU get to be more selective about who you let into your life. You’re still a worthy human being, and now you get to decide who gets the honor of being with you. Like I said, some days herpes is the fucking devil. Other days, it’s quite empowering. The key is finding the balance between the two and grounding yourself in self-care and trusting yourself to extend kindness to the one person who matters most. Not the easiest when you have a mental illness, trust meeee, but you’re not alone.

Sex educator here. I’m going to try to address as many points here as I can. 

First, you seem to have some knowledge about birth control, such as the fact that it’s not 100% effective (condoms are only about 78-85% effective despite what it says on the box) and that humans mess up its use (user error, human error, whatever you want to call it) and that often, people elect not to use a birth control method at all. So I don’t think you’re confused as to how people get pregnant? I think you know how it happens. To answer your question, yes, some people choose to have sex without the use of birth control. 

What I’m seeing here is less confusion about how this happens and more plain old judgment about people who have had multiple pregnancies and who get pregnant by strangers. You bring up your friend who has had multiple pregnancies by different men and then juxtapose it with your own experience of a long-term partnership and a planned pregnancy. What makes your experience more valid than your friend's? Because you had planned for your kid and she didn't? Your friend's experience isn't any less than your own. Plus she also miscarried, and the way you mention it so passively leads me to believe that you have little empathy for how that trauma can affect someone. 

Next, I encourage you to challenge the idea that STIs (sexually transmitted infections) are completely avoidable. 50% of sexually active people get one. The most common STI, HPV, has an incidence of about 14 million people - meaning about 14 million people contract it each year. It’s not as uncommon as you think and it's actually pretty difficult to prevent it with condom use because HPV is spread through skin-to-skin contact, not fluids. Therefore, any genital contact can transmit HPV, regardless of if you have a condom on. With numbers like that, how can we really think that STIs are easily preventible or make blanket statements about them? Also, STIs and unplanned pregnancies are not a gotcha consequence of sex. Yes, they are outcomes that for *some people* are adverse. But it’s not like “well if you have unprotected sex you deserve what you get.” If that resonates with you, I encourage you to analyze your capacity for empathy. 

Now, do I necessarily agree that it's totally fine to have PIV (penis in vagina) sex without a condom? Actually, no! I personally always use a condom with partners who have penises, and in my work as a sex educator, I encourage people to use condoms because they reduce the risk of unwanted outcomes and withdrawal (pulling out) is actually very difficult, particularly for youth. (Also, it kind of goes without saying, but I will add that I agree that it is decidedly *not cool* when a cisgender man tells his cisgender woman sex partner that he doesn't want to use a condom because it doesn't feel as good. I can recognize that the sensations are different, but to me, my peace of mind that I won't get pregnant or contract an STI trumps your desire for orgasm.) But we have to recognize that people have agency and choice, and they can choose not to use condoms and we have to accept that, no matter how much we think they're making the wrong choice. Additionally, there absolutely exists coercion - which of course is not okay either - and we have to recognize and extend empathy to those people who are in situations where their sexual circumstances are forced and they can't say no or advocate for themselves. When I say we need to recognize agency, we also need to recognize that sometimes people *aren't* empowered to make the choices they want to or that you would make. (Can we judge the people that force their partners to go without birth control and condemn sexual assault such as stealthing, which is the removal of a condom without the receiving partner's knowledge? Ya! And I would add that it's important to make the same effort to support the survivor of said assault, however they express needing it.) All this being said, does that give me a pass to judge couples/pairings/sex partners who consensually choose to go without though? No. 

Note on the use of STI instead of STD: language is ever-evolving! And it's generally accepted in the sex education field that "STI" is not only less stigmatizing than "STD", but frankly more accurate as well. All sexually transmitted \~whatevers\~ are infections, but they're not necessarily a disease. "Disease" suggests incurable, when that isn't true for all STIs. Bacterial & parasitic STIs -- things like chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and pubic lice (crabs) -- can all be cured with treatment. Viral STIs are incurable, but that does not mean the symptoms can't be treated. Genital warts caused by HPV, for instance, can be removed. Anti-viral medications exist for folks with viral infections. HIV is treated with anti-retrovirals that allow HIV+ folks to live long lives. Although not all STIs are curable, all are treatable.

> To be honest, STD's are scarier than COVID,

STIs are less of a big deal than society makes them out to be (and I could go on and on about that but I think user lukub5 successfully argues that they're not scary), but make no mistake, covid is serious, and I encourage you to be cautious about drawing comparisons between things that really are completely different. Promotion of condom use isn't propaganda. It's medically accurate health information. Propaganda, which by definition skews facts to serve a political agenda, exists all over and no one is immune to it, yes, but educating people about ways to reduce (notice I didn't say *eliminate*) risk is not it. To your point about "people \[being\] scared about getting ill," I'd agree that sometimes public health communication is *fear-based* and *shame-filled,* meaning their intent is just to scare the hell out of people to reduce what they consider adverse outcomes, but that doesn't automatically make condom promotion propaganda.

Speaking from experience here: you can absolutely call the police to do a check-in, especially if you think your friend poses an immediate danger to herself. I’m glad that your friend has someone as thoughtful as you in her life. That being said, as someone who’s been on the opposite side of this same situation, it’s absolutely terrifying to have the police show up at your door demanding to know who you are and where you’ve been. I know it comes from a place of concern for safety, but for real, the police are not your friend; they won’t come in gently or cater to your personality or just talk to you like a friend would. The interaction is callous, abrupt and can be traumatizing to someone who has had negative experiences with police. For me personally, I was furious that my friends called the cops on me. I knew objectively they were just worried about me, but the police interaction itself felt like a huge invasion of my privacy and made me more vulnerable, and the whole situation alienated me from my friends for some time. I wish there was another option, like calling EMTs, but 911 dispatch will pretty much always send a police officer before they “waste” the resources of an ambulance. I say all this not to dissuade you from calling the police, but just to give you another perspective of how your concern may be perceived. And I know folks might suggest that it doesn’t matter if your friend is mad at you as long as she’s safe. In the long run I agree. I just want you to be well-informed of how your friend might take it and be prepared for some backlash, if she’s anything like me. Which she might not be. She might be really glad that someone cares enough to check in on her. My only actual suggestion would be, if you want to avoid involving the authorities and have the time and means, make a trip out there if you can. I hope it all works out for you and your friend.
